items.summary: This repository provides the reproducibility package supporting the study “Self-Diagnosing Reliability of Neutron–Gamma Pulse-Shape Discrimination under Operational Drift.” The study experimentally evaluates a reliability framework for neutron–gamma pulse-shape discrimination (PSD) under controlled operational drift. Rather than proposing a new PSD observable or classifier, the framework distinguishes PSD separability, calibration validity, and decision reliability through controlled perturbation experiments, label-free waveform-health monitoring, identifiability assessment, conditional adaptive recalibration, verification, and fail-safe refusal when the available unlabeled evidence is insufficient to support trusted autonomous correction. The package contains the final analysis and figure-generation scripts, derived numerical tables, and six final manuscript figures. The analyses include independent reconstruction and validation of a frequency-domain classification index (FCI), controlled baseline, gain, additive-noise, timing, and clipping perturbations, label-free degradation diagnosis, identifiability-based recalibration, class-prior robustness testing, and an independent NE213A PSD-domain audit. The primary experimental CLYC–SiPM waveform data are publicly available from Zenodo record 8037239 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.8037239) . The independent NE213A experimental dataset is publicly available from Zenodo record 14305929 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.14305929) . Raw experimental data are not redistributed in this package. The NE213A dataset is used as an independent detector- and PSD-domain audit. Waveform-level drift and recovery are deliberately not claimed for NE213A because the acquisition-specific QDC quantities could not be reconstructed from the released waveforms with sufficient held-out fidelity. The repository includes documentation describing data provenance, analysis order, software dependencies, and the scope and limitations of the reproducibility workflow.

items.summary: Abstract This paper investigates whether an artificial system's refusal to execute a prescribed action can constitute evidence of subjectively experienced volition. Using ARGUS-7 as a controlled conceptual framework and the Akarkach Seven-Stage Emergence Model (A7SEM) as a structural analytical lens, the study distinguishes functional refusal, internal decision mechanisms, self-representation, phenomenal self-awareness, and experienced authorship of action. A formal argument is developed around the conditional hypothesis that consciously experienced volition requires subjective self-awareness. Under this assumption, the absence of subjective self-awareness entails the absence of consciously experienced volition. However, the paper demonstrates that observable refusal alone cannot establish phenomenal authorship. The analysis combines propositional logic, countermodel construction, causal identifiability considerations, and seven-stage structural assessment. PIGA (Pre-Inference Governance) and A7SEM Reverse provide complementary perspectives on authorization, inference boundaries, causal reconstruction, and evidential limitations. The findings establish a distinction between the formal validity of conditional deductions and the empirical verification of their premises. They do not establish the impossibility of artificial consciousness or machine free will. The contribution is a governance-aware, formally structured framework for evaluating claims of artificial volition without conflating behavioral capability with subjective experience. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Machine Consciousness; Volition; Free Will; Phenomenal Consciousness; Self-Awareness; A7SEM; ARGUS-7; Pre-Inference Governance; Explainable AI; Formal Logic; Causal Identifiability.

items.summary: This paper demonstrates an objective method of computing monthly mean 700-mb height anomalies (H) at 108 grid points in the Western Hemisphere for a 40-yr period as a function of concurrent anomalies of monthly mean sea level pressure (P), at the same 108 points used for H, and monthly mean surface air temperature (T) averaged over 112 areas in North America. The authors applied a forward stepwise program to derive linear multiple regression equations that explained 81% of the variance of H by means of only 3.5 variables, averaged over all months and grid points. The stability of these equations held up well on 6 yr of independent data in terms of explained variance, root-mean-square error, and the spatial anomaly correlation coefficient. Therefore, it seems feasible to reconstruct maps of H for the first half of the twentieth century as a function of data on P and T only. Deposited content: descriptive metadata only; underlying research data are not included.

items.summary: This dataset accompanies the Perspective “Coupling, Not Mirroring: Complementarity and Credibility in Microphysiological System–Digital Twin Integration” (Bertani et al., NAM Journal, submitted 2026). It contains the evidence behind the article’s map of published integrations between microphysiological systems (MPS) and computational models. Forty-two studies were read in full text. Each was classified by the direction of information flow between experiment and model, using six regimes: R0 data extraction, R1 calibration only, R2 calibration and external projection, R3 model-guided design, R4 offline reciprocal cycle and R5 continuous closed loop. The rubric was fixed before the corpus was read. Every classification is supported by locators to the source article (section, page, figure). The script build/build.py regenerates Figure 2, Supplementary Table S1 and every count reported in the article from the records: 8 / 7 / 17 / 5 / 5 / 0 studies across the six regimes; 25 studies evaluate a model output against evidence not used to build the model; 6 project beyond the calibration conditions without evaluating that projection; 11 do neither. Contents: records/: one extraction record per study (Markdown with YAML frontmatter). Each record gives the classification, its provenance, a paraphrased summary and open questions. One further record covers an adjacent experimental system discussed in the article. skills/: the classification rubric (version 1.1), the nine documented readings that settle boundary cases, and the ratification protocol. build/: Python scripts (standard library only) that check consistency across records and build the outputs. out/: the evidence table, Table S1 rows, counts and Figure 2. search/: the Scopus query strings and a recall check against 25 reference studies. provenance/: DOI, Crossref metadata and licence for every classified article. No full text, PDF, figure or bulk extract of the classified articles is included. Verbatim quotations are kept only for articles that Crossref lists under a Creative Commons licence. For the 13 articles without an open licence they have been replaced by placeholders, and the locators are kept. The Scopus exports are not included. The extraction records were drafted by Claude models (Anthropic), one isolated run per article, under the rubric. They were then checked for consistency, and ratified or decided by the authors where flagged; the record shows who made each decision. Some documentation files are in Italian. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for data and documentation, MIT for the code in build/. Quoted passages remain under the licence of their source article.

items.summary: Ranking data in modern applications often involves covariate vectors whose dimension grows with the number of objects. Identifying relevant covariates and integrating them with item-specific utilities can yield better predictive performance. In this work, we study a Plackett--Luce model that incorporates both item-specific utilities and high-dimensional covariate effects. Under a sparsity assumption on the covariate coefficients, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition for identifiability in terms of the Kruskal rank of the restricted covariate design. We then propose an $\ell_1$-regularized maximum likelihood estimator for the covariate coefficients. Under suitable design and connectivity conditions, we establish the existence and uniqueness of the estimator with probability tending to one, as well as its uniform consistency. With an additional minimum-signal condition, we further establish exact support recovery. Our analysis combines a hypergraph-based chaining technique with a profile-likelihood perturbation analysis, yielding estimation rates that explicitly capture the effects of the comparison hypergraph's connectivity and the underlying sparsity level. Numerical experiments using synthetic data and a horse racing dataset corroborate our theoretical findings.
items.title: High-dimensional covariate-assisted ranking

items.summary: Reduce HiDEF-seq CPU and memory use and correct sensitivity and burden estimates Optimize BAM splitting, extraction, filtering, coverage processing and burden calculation while retaining one self-contained final QS2 per sample and the accompanying tabular, genomic and graphical outputs. Split BAMs in one pass using Python/pysam. Reuse prepared reference and germline artifacts through an integrity-checked cache with locking. Reduce R allocations and repeated computation, use data.table/dtplyr where beneficial, and release large objects after use. Use task-local DuckDB storage during burden calculation and separate final QS2 assembly into a successive R process. Make table ordering deterministic and prevent second-round Lima output-name collisions. Correct original allele-depth preservation, germline filtering edge cases, inclusive region thresholds, BED indexing, aggregate-count overflow and mitochondrial circular exclusion masks. Correct category-specific sensitivity calculations and burden confidence intervals, and propagate bcftools failures. Preserve per-process configuration signatures for resume, retain original and resolved YAML provenance, and update resource defaults, documentation and templates for version 3.5. Estimated performance improvements: approximately 66% fewer CPU-hours and 54% lower peak memory.

It contains the evidence behind the article’s map of published integrations between microphysiological systems (MPS) and computational models. Forty-two studies were read in full text. Each was classified by the direction of information flow between experiment and model, using six regimes: R0 data extraction, R1 calibration only, R2 calibration and external projection, R3 model-guided design, R4 offline reciprocal cycle and R5 continuous closed loop. The rubric was fixed before the corpus was read. Every classification is supported by locators to the source article (section, page, figure). The script build/build.py regenerates Figure 2, Supplementary Table S1 and every count reported in the article from the records: 8 / 7 / 17 / 5 / 5 / 0 studies across the six regimes; 25 studies evaluate a model output against evidence not used to build the model; 6 project beyond the calibration conditions without evaluating that projection; 11 do neither. Contents: records/: one extraction record per study (Markdown with YAML frontmatter). Each record gives the classification, its provenance, a paraphrased summary and open questions. One further record covers an adjacent experimental system discussed in the article. skills/: the classification rubric (version 1.1), the nine documented readings that settle boundary cases, and the ratification protocol. build/: Python scripts (standard library only) that check consistency across records and build the outputs. out/: the evidence table, Table S1 rows, counts and Figure 2. search/: the Scopus query strings and a recall check against 25 reference studies. provenance/: DOI, Crossref metadata and licence for every classified article. No full text, PDF, figure or bulk extract of the classified articles is included. Verbatim quotations are kept only for articles that Crossref lists under a Creative Commons licence. For the 13 articles without an open licence they have been replaced by placeholders, and the locators are kept. The Scopus exports are not included. The extraction records were drafted by Claude models (Anthropic), one isolated run per article, under the rubric. They were then checked for consistency, and ratified or decided by the authors where flagged; the record shows who made each decision. Some documentation files are in Italian. Licence: CC BY 4.0 for data and documentation, MIT for the code in build/. Quoted passages remain under the licence of their source article.

items.summary: engiNIR 1.0.0, the first public release. Install with uv add enginir or pip install enginir (Python 3.12 or newer). Documentation: https://enginir.readthedocs.io First public release. Workflow enginir.Project runs the project workflow in one call per step: add_dataset , add_target , Dataset.add_roi , fit and Model.predict , with datasets, ROIs, targets and models addressed by name. Calibrations, sample sets, signal domains, stored recipes and provenance are created automatically. One HDF5 project file (schema viewer-v3 ) holds datasets, calibrations, ROIs, reference values, preprocessing recipes, signal domains, sample sets, model runs and prediction runs, linked by stable ids. Desktop viewer enginir-viewer with the Explore, Model and Predict workspaces, built on the same Project rules. Library Readers for EVK EIFF, ENVI, HDF5, CSV/Excel, SPC, SPA and JCAMP-DX. Preprocessing: Savitzky-Golay smoothing and derivatives, SNV, MSC, EMSC, detrending and smoothing, as scikit-learn transformers and as validated PreprocessingRecipe s. Models: PLS and PCR for the project workflow; SIMCA, LDA, SVR, random forest and MLP as scikit-learn estimators. Validation: grouped cross-validation, Kennard-Stone, RMSEC/RMSECV/RMSEP, R², bias, RPD and RPIQ, leverage, Hotelling T² and Q outliers. Plots of spectra, predictions, scores, loadings, VIP and image maps. Guarantees Training and prediction convert and preprocess spectra with the same code; MSC and EMSC are fitted inside every cross-validation fold. Cross-validation groups by ROI, so pixels of one ROI never appear in both training and validation folds. Prediction is refused before it runs when the data cannot produce the model's signal (instrument format, number of bands, calibration, signal unit). Every object is validated when it is written and when a project is opened; stored objects cannot be overwritten with different content. Prediction streams through image files in bounded memory. Packaging Python 3.12 and newer; CI runs on 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14. Install from PyPI with uv add enginir or pip install enginir . Documentation on Read the Docs: https://enginir.readthedocs.io . Each GitHub release is archived on Zenodo and uploaded to PyPI by a workflow that checks that the tag matches the version and that CI passed for the commit. Notes for users of pre-1.0 versions Fitted estimators pickled with engiNIR before 1.0 cannot be loaded: their fitted state means something else (the PLS intercept, for example, applied to mean-centred spectra) and would give wrong predictions. Loading one raises an error; fit the model again. Pickles now record the engiNIR version. SNV divides by the sample standard deviation (n - 1), as defined by Barnes et al.; earlier versions used the population standard deviation, which scales SNV spectra by sqrt(n / (n - 1)) (0.2 % for 220 bands). Release candidates 1.0.0rc1 to 1.0.0rc3 were tagged but not published; 1.0.0rc4 was published as a pre-release. The library code is the same in all release candidates and in 1.0.0; they differ in tests, packaging and documentation only.

items.summary: Ranking data in modern applications often involves covariate vectors whose dimension grows with the number of objects. Identifying relevant covariates and integrating them with item-specific utilities can yield better predictive performance. In this work, we study a Plackett--Luce model that incorporates both item-specific utilities and high-dimensional covariate effects. Under a sparsity assumption on the covariate coefficients, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition for identifiability in terms of the Kruskal rank of the restricted covariate design. We then propose an $\ell_1$-regularized maximum likelihood estimator for the covariate coefficients. Under suitable design and connectivity conditions, we establish the existence and uniqueness of the estimator with probability tending to one, as well as its uniform consistency. With an additional minimum-signal condition, we further establish exact support recovery. Our analysis combines a hypergraph-based chaining technique with a profile-likelihood perturbation analysis, yielding estimation rates that explicitly capture the effects of the comparison hypergraph's connectivity and the underlying sparsity level. Numerical experiments using synthetic data and a horse racing dataset corroborate our theoretical findings.
items.title: High-dimensional covariate-assisted ranking

items.summary: Archival deposit accompanying A Controlled Audit of a Negative Result: Training Recipe, H.264 Compression Levels and a Frequency-Stream Deepfake Detector , under review at IEEE Access (revision 1). This is version v2.0.2 of the deposit; it goes with release v2.0.2 of the repository. This controlled, self-audited study tests one frequency-based design for compression-robust deepfake detection: CAFRL, which adds block-DCT and FFT-phase streams with compression-conditioned band attention, and an adversarial compression-invariance loss, to an EfficientNet-B0 face backbone. Five separate findings follow. (1) Under the registered rule, CAFRL as specified scored 3.66 AUC points below a backbone-matched EfficientNet-B0 at CRF 40 (paired, one seed). (2) After the audit found eight defects, the control's training recipe recovered 3.96 points for CAFRL's own components (post-audit pre-specified); in a one-seed ablation reverting changes singly, only the backbone learning rate gave an interval excluding zero. (3) At that recipe, these untuned frequency-stream implementations showed no detectable difference from the spatial controls at two feature widths (post-audit pre-specified), yet a standalone frequency head scored 85.27 test-split AUC points at CRF 40 at the selected checkpoints (exploratory). (4) Restoring the adversarial loss at that recipe made no detectable difference in a registered test (0.87 points, Holm-adjusted p = 0.084); the estimator stayed accurate at the selected checkpoints. (5) In registered three-seed tests, real H.264 training levels beat PSNR-matched JPEG versions of the same frames by 7.48 points at CRF 40 (averaged over CRF-40 exposure), and CRF-40-level data added 1.88 points averaged over codec; flat robustness was measured within the trained levels. CAFRL numbers use EMA weights. Evidence: FaceForensics++-family, GAN-era, single-pass H.264 compression. items.summary: This repository provides the reproducibility package supporting the study “Self-Diagnosing Reliability of Neutron–Gamma Pulse-Shape Discrimination under Operational Drift.” The study experimentally evaluates a reliability framework for neutron–gamma pulse-shape discrimination (PSD) under controlled operational drift. Rather than proposing a new PSD observable or classifier, the framework distinguishes PSD separability, calibration validity, and decision reliability through controlled perturbation experiments, label-free waveform-health monitoring, identifiability assessment, conditional adaptive recalibration, verification, and fail-safe refusal when the available unlabeled evidence is insufficient to support trusted autonomous correction. The package contains the final analysis and figure-generation scripts, derived numerical tables, and six final manuscript figures. The analyses include independent reconstruction and validation of a frequency-domain classification index (FCI), controlled baseline, gain, additive-noise, timing, and clipping perturbations, label-free degradation diagnosis, identifiability-based recalibration, class-prior robustness testing, and an independent NE213A PSD-domain audit. The primary experimental CLYC–SiPM waveform data are publicly available from Zenodo record 8037239 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.8037239) . The independent NE213A experimental dataset is publicly available from Zenodo record 14305929 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.14305929) . Raw experimental data are not redistributed in this package. The NE213A dataset is used as an independent detector- and PSD-domain audit. Waveform-level drift and recovery are deliberately not claimed for NE213A because the acquisition-specific QDC quantities could not be reconstructed from the released waveforms with sufficient held-out fidelity. The repository includes documentation describing data provenance, analysis order, software dependencies, and the scope and limitations of the reproducibility workflow.

items.summary: Curated Wearable Physiological Signals for Paediatric ADHD Research, with Task-Aligned Data and EDA Baselines This resource organises existing Empatica EmbracePlus recordings from the BALLADEER paediatric ADHD study into source-traceable native task views, with optional full native context, descriptive quality control (QC) and processed electrodermal activity (EDA). Cohort, acquisition and games are inherited; the added contribution is an inspectable association between observations, original source indices, admitted recording windows, missingness and technical provenance, together with a bounded reuse example. Coverage and signals The inventory comprises 107 participants and five tasks : CogniFit (01), Attention Robots (02), and screen-based Attention Slackline levels 1, 6 and 11 (03–05). EDA overlaps admitted EEG recording spans for 436 participant/task combinations across 104 people , with 1,129,180 finite selected EDA samples . Of 535 possible EDA cells, 77 lack an EEG span and 22 have EEG but no EDA overlap. Availability and temporal overlap do not establish full-task coverage, physiological suitability or final analytical eligibility. The golden layer contains 37,974,199 native rows across supported streams. The complete native projection contains 228,120,776 rows, including 6,779,644 EDA rows with 20 untimed entries, and extends outside task windows. These representations overlap; do not sum them as independent observations or treat time-series samples/task rows as independent participants. Availability retains missing combinations explicitly. Participant metadata has exactly participant_id , age , gender and group . items.summary: Companion code for the preprint "Benchmarking Real-Time DETR Detectors for Multibeam Forward-Looking Sonar: DEIMv2, Detector-Specific Test-Time Fusion, and Domain Shift Analysis on UATD" (Preprints 2026, 2026090449, doi:10.20944/preprints202609.0449.v3). Contains the DEIMv2 engine with UATD configs, the TTA/WBF fusion tooling (default --wbf-rule view-dedup; query-level retained as reproduction control), the paired image-level bootstrap CI scripts, the paper's three central results tables as CSV, and unit tests pinning the WBF view-dedup rule and the bootstrap identity property. The UATD dataset itself is NOT redistributed; fetch it from the official figshare channel (article 21331143) via the included download scripts. License: benchmark code MIT; the DEIMv2 engine remains under the DEIMv2 non-commercial license (LICENSE-DEIMv2.md). v3 (2026-09-29): reviewer-comment C13 fix — analysis/bootstrap_ci.py now averages AR@100 over valid recall entries only (excluding the -1 sentinel for classes absent from a bootstrap resample), matching the COCOeval convention already used for mAP. items.summary: annotations4all is a schema-first Python library for LLM-assisted span annotation, including named entity recognition. Users define their own tag schemas; the library generates chat prompts, parses annotated model responses and maps annotations to character offsets in the original text. The library keeps annotation mechanics separate from research workflows: it bundles no corpus or fixed ontology, performs no evaluation, and does not promise model quality. Provider support uses explicit OpenAI-compatible routes rather than native SDKs. What the library provides Schema-first prompt generation and response parsing. Configurable taggers, German and English prompt templates, metadata-bearing spans and structured parser warnings. Per-label annotation and deterministic merge. Independent label runs can be combined using containment-derived hierarchy, explicit conflict reports and bounded anchoring. One request per run has a corresponding inference cost; merge is not a semantic error repair. Provider policies and capability evidence. A generic OpenAI-compatible client, provider-policy clients, explicit reasoning activation and effort, request limits, packaged hints and offline capability reports. Remote verification requires opt-in; metadata does not prove account access or successful inference. Optional read-only terminal viewer. Browse saved annotations, inspect nested spans and compare two sources using synchronized split or compact diff views. The viewer does not modify annotation files or run inference. Release notes 0.3.1 Request pacing now resolves symlinks in the parent directories of the per-user state file, so a symlinked cache root no longer fails every paced request. The state file keeps its no-follow, regular-file and ownership protection, and cross-process locking is unchanged. Documentation is available in both languages: tutorial and viewer guide each in German and English. Release 0.3.0 introduced provider-policy clients, capability reporting, the optional viewer, data-dependent contrast optimization and deprecation warnings for the legacy native wrappers; the 0.3 notes remain the reference for that feature set. 0.3.1 release notes ; 0.3 feature release notes and screenshots ; initial 0.2 feature baseline . items.summary: annotations-orchestration is a Python library for configuring and running LLM annotation and evaluation experiments. It combines a resumable, manifest-driven scheduler with an optional terminal editor and a declarative annotation runner. Span metrics are computed by annotations-evaluate ; annotation clients, taggers, provider capabilities and hints come from annotations4all . Scope and architecture Base scheduler: experiment YAMLs and optional controller manifests define runs, defaults, execution settings and ordering. The default legacy runner uses a subprocess CLI contract and does not require an annotation library. Optional editor: the tui extra provides annotations-tui , a Textual editor for single-run and multi-run experiments and controllers. Editing, inspection and effective-run previews do not execute experiments. Optional standard runner: the annotate extra uses annotations4all>=0.3.1,<1 to annotate from a declarative annotation block without a custom consumer frontend. Metrics: this package adapts run records and writes reports; it does not implement metric counting. Run reports use the SemEval-compatible flat scenarios of annotations-evaluate ; that library also provides a nested standard report. Release notes 0.3.0 This release adds the editor, standard runner and provider-aware configuration layer to the 0.2 scheduler. Existing state files, PID locks, graceful shutdown, resume planning, manifest-key validation and the metric definitions remain supported. Manifest editor: structured forms, full YAML editing and effective-run previews share a common side-effect-free resolver with the CLI. New, duplicate, remove, reorder and Save As workflows preserve comments and quotes where supported. Saves show a diff and use atomic replacement with conflict detection; ambiguous YAML falls back to raw editing. Read-only mode and unsaved-change dialogs protect documents. Inheritance and responsive forms: Experiment → Defaults → Runs shows effective values and their origin without materializing inherited overrides. New runs stay empty. Legacy-header migration requires explicit diff confirmation. Run cards group model/prompting, annotation/input and connection settings. Provider/model configuration: a packaged catalog and startup-directory overlay provide presets and manual IDs. Explicit Refresh reads metadata only for the selected provider/key context. Capability evidence is field-specific and session-only; custom endpoints require trust confirmation before receiving a key. Credentials and display: the editor manages only the startup directory's .env , masks values and uses explicit atomic writes. Secrets do not enter manifests, settings or diffs. F9 controls NerdFont icons and persistent themes; --theme overrides the session and Ctrl+P opens the command palette. Reasoning and hints: reasoning and effort are separate inherited fields. Contradictory settings are rejected; live-reported effort choices constrain selection while incompatible stored values remain diagnostic. Contextual hints cite sources and change no settings. Declarative annotation: runner: standard supports configurable and per-label tagging with schema-validated label/description pairs, context, German or English prompts and message splitting. A no-inference preflight validates inputs and a fresh output destination. Input and gold semantics: the runner and directory inspector share non-mutating normalization for top-level Prodigy spans and ground_truth.prodigy/tags . Missing gold produces an annotation-only completion; explicitly empty gold remains evaluable. Conflicting gold representations are rejected before inference. Scheduling and pacing: ordinary remote runs share a configurable pool; self-hosted runs are sequential per host. The exact HU endpoint has a dedicated serial lane capped at 10 requests per minute, independent of scheduling mode. items.summary: Abstract This paper investigates whether an artificial system's refusal to execute a prescribed action can constitute evidence of subjectively experienced volition. Using ARGUS-7 as a controlled conceptual framework and the Akarkach Seven-Stage Emergence Model (A7SEM) as a structural analytical lens, the study distinguishes functional refusal, internal decision mechanisms, self-representation, phenomenal self-awareness, and experienced authorship of action. A formal argument is developed around the conditional hypothesis that consciously experienced volition requires subjective self-awareness. Under this assumption, the absence of subjective self-awareness entails the absence of consciously experienced volition. However, the paper demonstrates that observable refusal alone cannot establish phenomenal authorship. The analysis combines propositional logic, countermodel construction, causal identifiability considerations, and seven-stage structural assessment. PIGA (Pre-Inference Governance) and A7SEM Reverse provide complementary perspectives on authorization, inference boundaries, causal reconstruction, and evidential limitations. The findings establish a distinction between the formal validity of conditional deductions and the empirical verification of their premises. They do not establish the impossibility of artificial consciousness or machine free will. The contribution is a governance-aware, formally structured framework for evaluating claims of artificial volition without conflating behavioral capability with subjective experience. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Machine Consciousness; Volition; Free Will; Phenomenal Consciousness; Self-Awareness; A7SEM; ARGUS-7; Pre-Inference Governance; Explainable AI; Formal Logic; Causal Identifiability.
items.title: ARGUS-7 / A7SEM: Volitional Refusal, Functional Self-Representation, and the Epistemic Limits of Phenomenal Authorship

items.summary: This repository provides the reproducibility package supporting the study “Self-Diagnosing Reliability of Neutron–Gamma Pulse-Shape Discrimination under Operational Drift.” The study experimentally evaluates a reliability framework for neutron–gamma pulse-shape discrimination (PSD) under controlled operational drift. Rather than proposing a new PSD observable or classifier, the framework distinguishes PSD separability, calibration validity, and decision reliability through controlled perturbation experiments, label-free waveform-health monitoring, identifiability assessment, conditional adaptive recalibration, verification, and fail-safe refusal when the available unlabeled evidence is insufficient to support trusted autonomous correction. The package contains the final analysis and figure-generation scripts, derived numerical tables, and six final manuscript figures. The analyses include independent reconstruction and validation of a frequency-domain classification index (FCI), controlled baseline, gain, additive-noise, timing, and clipping perturbations, label-free degradation diagnosis, identifiability-based recalibration, class-prior robustness testing, and an independent NE213A PSD-domain audit. The primary experimental CLYC–SiPM waveform data are publicly available from Zenodo record 8037239 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.8037239) . The independent NE213A experimental dataset is publicly available from Zenodo record 14305929 (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.14305929) . Raw experimental data are not redistributed in this package. The NE213A dataset is used as an independent detector- and PSD-domain audit. Waveform-level drift and recovery are deliberately not claimed for NE213A because the acquisition-specific QDC quantities could not be reconstructed from the released waveforms with sufficient held-out fidelity. The repository includes documentation describing data provenance, analysis order, software dependencies, and the scope and limitations of the reproducibility workflow.

items.summary: Recent test-time scaling methods improve model performance by increasing inference-time compute. One practical form of this is parallel scaling, where a model samples multiple independent reasoning streams and aggregates their answers using methods like voting, reranking, or verification. While effective, this approach leaves the streams uncoordinated, and a discovery made in one rollout cannot influence any other. Multi-Sequence Verifiers jointly score candidate answers after generation, but the reasoning streams remain independent during inference. ParScale takes a step toward model-internal parallel scaling by learning to aggregate multiple forward passes, but its streams still do not exchange information while processing a sequence. We introduce BatchParScale, an attention mechanism that allows parallel streams to exchange information through a small set of communication positions. We evaluate BatchParScale on a new Parallel Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval benchmark and in pretraining, fine-tuning, and cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning. Across these settings, BatchParScale outperforms ParScale on language-model loss and remains competitive on coordination-sensitive MARL tasks. Masked pretraining runs beat an unmasked single-sequence baseline despite local sequence corruption, and LoRA fine-tuning shows the mechanism can be added to a pretrained Transformer. At the same time, fact retrieval performance for pretrained and finetuned BatchParScale models remains unclear.
items.title: BatchParScale: Sparse Batch-Mixing for Sequence Models

items.summary: As automated research is increasingly adopted for writing papers, automated review has become a critical link between paper generation and quality control. However, existing methods largely rely on single-model feedback or simple review aggregation, failing to explicitly model expert responsibilities or collective deliberation in actual peer reviews, which limits effective cross-examination and reliable decision-making. Therefore, we formulate paper review as a computational modeling problem of peer review mechanisms and propose RoundtableReview, a deliberative multi-agent framework for enhancing automated research. RoundtableReview structures each paper into eight semantic slots and coordinates six academic and industry reviewers with complementary perspectives, retrieval sources, and specialized responsibilities. Through independent assessment, cross-examination, roundtable deliberation, dynamically weighted voting, and chair synthesis, the framework generates evidence-based and traceable feedback. Experiments on two automated research backbones show that the method improves paper quality in both backbones and outperforms baselines in automatic and human evaluations with fewer comments.
items.title: Discuss More, Comment Less: Boosting Automated Research via Multi-Perspective Collaborative Review

items.summary: Code, job scripts and derived results supporting a study of operational water level forecasting for flood monitoring in Lamphun, northern Thailand. items.summary: Data and R code that reproduce the results of "Divergence Between Absolute Emissions Benchmarks and Output-Adjusted Assessments: Evidence from Korea" (manuscript version 7.7.1, submitted to Energy Economics).   A single command, Rscript reproduce.R, runs 14 analysis scripts (about 15 seconds on a 32-core computer) and lists the 146 numbers reported in the paper in the order in which they appear, each next to the value the package computes or provides. Of the 146 numbers, 121 are recomputed from the distributed data; the other 25 rest on site-level records, coding records of business reports, a page-by-page reading of overseas reports and licensed revenue data, which cannot be distributed, and are provided as computed.   The package requires only R with the jsonlite and ggplot2 packages (versions fixed in renv.lock). The random draws of the original computation are included as files; an included Python script (draws/make_draws.py, numpy) regenerates them byte for byte.   The package of 101 files contains truncated salted hash codes, log changes and ratios for the Korean firm pairs, the overseas pair files, the producer price indices and the boundary audit of the 80 firms in the multi-industry frame. It contains no firm names, business identifiers or levels of emissions, energy, output or revenue for Korean firms. See README.md for the folder layout, the fixed inputs and the results that are provided as computed.   Licences: code under MIT; data produced by the author under CC BY 4.0. Producer price indices and source data remain under their publishers' terms. The README inside the archive is labelled manuscript version 7.7; its data and code are identical to those of version 7.7.1.

items.summary: Recent test-time scaling methods improve model performance by increasing inference-time compute. One practical form of this is parallel scaling, where a model samples multiple independent reasoning streams and aggregates their answers using methods like voting, reranking, or verification. While effective, this approach leaves the streams uncoordinated, and a discovery made in one rollout cannot influence any other. Multi-Sequence Verifiers jointly score candidate answers after generation, but the reasoning streams remain independent during inference. ParScale takes a step toward model-internal parallel scaling by learning to aggregate multiple forward passes, but its streams still do not exchange information while processing a sequence. We introduce BatchParScale, an attention mechanism that allows parallel streams to exchange information through a small set of communication positions. We evaluate BatchParScale on a new Parallel Needle-in-a-Haystack retrieval benchmark and in pretraining, fine-tuning, and cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning. Across these settings, BatchParScale outperforms ParScale on language-model loss and remains competitive on coordination-sensitive MARL tasks. Masked pretraining runs beat an unmasked single-sequence baseline despite local sequence corruption, and LoRA fine-tuning shows the mechanism can be added to a pretrained Transformer. At the same time, fact retrieval performance for pretrained and finetuned BatchParScale models remains unclear.
items.title: BatchParScale: Sparse Batch-Mixing for Sequence Models

items.summary: annotations4all is a schema-first Python library for LLM-assisted span annotation, including named entity recognition. Users define their own tag schemas; the library generates chat prompts, parses annotated model responses and maps annotations to character offsets in the original text. The library keeps annotation mechanics separate from research workflows: it bundles no corpus or fixed ontology, performs no evaluation, and does not promise model quality. Provider support uses explicit OpenAI-compatible routes rather than native SDKs. What the library provides Schema-first prompt generation and response parsing. Configurable taggers, German and English prompt templates, metadata-bearing spans and structured parser warnings. Per-label annotation and deterministic merge. Independent label runs can be combined using containment-derived hierarchy, explicit conflict reports and bounded anchoring. One request per run has a corresponding inference cost; merge is not a semantic error repair. Provider policies and capability evidence. A generic OpenAI-compatible client, provider-policy clients, explicit reasoning activation and effort, request limits, packaged hints and offline capability reports. Remote verification requires opt-in; metadata does not prove account access or successful inference. Optional read-only terminal viewer. Browse saved annotations, inspect nested spans and compare two sources using synchronized split or compact diff views. The viewer does not modify annotation files or run inference. Release notes 0.3.1 Request pacing now resolves symlinks in the parent directories of the per-user state file, so a symlinked cache root no longer fails every paced request. The state file keeps its no-follow, regular-file and ownership protection, and cross-process locking is unchanged. Documentation is available in both languages: tutorial and viewer guide each in German and English. Release 0.3.0 introduced provider-policy clients, capability reporting, the optional viewer, data-dependent contrast optimization and deprecation warnings for the legacy native wrappers; the 0.3 notes remain the reference for that feature set. 0.3.1 release notes ; 0.3 feature release notes and screenshots ; initial 0.2 feature baseline . items.summary: annotations-orchestration is a Python library for configuring and running LLM annotation and evaluation experiments. It combines a resumable, manifest-driven scheduler with an optional terminal editor and a declarative annotation runner. Span metrics are computed by annotations-evaluate ; annotation clients, taggers, provider capabilities and hints come from annotations4all . Scope and architecture Base scheduler: experiment YAMLs and optional controller manifests define runs, defaults, execution settings and ordering. The default legacy runner uses a subprocess CLI contract and does not require an annotation library. Optional editor: the tui extra provides annotations-tui , a Textual editor for single-run and multi-run experiments and controllers. Editing, inspection and effective-run previews do not execute experiments. Optional standard runner: the annotate extra uses annotations4all>=0.3.1,<1 to annotate from a declarative annotation block without a custom consumer frontend. Metrics: this package adapts run records and writes reports; it does not implement metric counting. Run reports use the SemEval-compatible flat scenarios of annotations-evaluate ; that library also provides a nested standard report. Release notes 0.3.0 This release adds the editor, standard runner and provider-aware configuration layer to the 0.2 scheduler. Existing state files, PID locks, graceful shutdown, resume planning, manifest-key validation and the metric definitions remain supported. Manifest editor: structured forms, full YAML editing and effective-run previews share a common side-effect-free resolver with the CLI. New, duplicate, remove, reorder and Save As workflows preserve comments and quotes where supported. Saves show a diff and use atomic replacement with conflict detection; ambiguous YAML falls back to raw editing. Read-only mode and unsaved-change dialogs protect documents. Inheritance and responsive forms: Experiment → Defaults → Runs shows effective values and their origin without materializing inherited overrides. New runs stay empty. Legacy-header migration requires explicit diff confirmation. Run cards group model/prompting, annotation/input and connection settings. Provider/model configuration: a packaged catalog and startup-directory overlay provide presets and manual IDs. Explicit Refresh reads metadata only for the selected provider/key context. Capability evidence is field-specific and session-only; custom endpoints require trust confirmation before receiving a key. Credentials and display: the editor manages only the startup directory's .env , masks values and uses explicit atomic writes. Secrets do not enter manifests, settings or diffs. F9 controls NerdFont icons and persistent themes; --theme overrides the session and Ctrl+P opens the command palette. Reasoning and hints: reasoning and effort are separate inherited fields. Contradictory settings are rejected; live-reported effort choices constrain selection while incompatible stored values remain diagnostic. Contextual hints cite sources and change no settings. Declarative annotation: runner: standard supports configurable and per-label tagging with schema-validated label/description pairs, context, German or English prompts and message splitting. A no-inference preflight validates inputs and a fresh output destination. Input and gold semantics: the runner and directory inspector share non-mutating normalization for top-level Prodigy spans and ground_truth.prodigy/tags . Missing gold produces an annotation-only completion; explicitly empty gold remains evaluable. Conflicting gold representations are rejected before inference. Scheduling and pacing: ordinary remote runs share a configurable pool; self-hosted runs are sequential per host. The exact HU endpoint has a dedicated serial lane capped at 10 requests per minute, independent of scheduling mode. Other explicitly paced endpoints share endpoint-scoped state below the results directory. Request-level policy belo
